title: Burst Orchestrator: IaC Safety Catalog and Deployment Validation
author: Connor Mitchell
content:
Summary:
This document catalogs the Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) patterns, validation gates, and operational runbook for the Burst Orchestrator: a policy layer and Terraform module set that coordinates GPU burst capacity across spot, warm-pool, and reserved clusters while enforcing network egress and tenant isolation constraints. It is intended for infra engineers owning GPU provisioning, cloud networking, and the CI/CD runners that deploy these modules.

Goals and scope:
- Provide a single reference for module variants, safety checks, and rollout patterns used when enabling burst capacity or adding new cluster flavors.
- Ensure every change to allocator iac has automated terraform plan checks, policy-as-code gates, and a deterministic rollback path.
- Reduce noisy-neighbor incidents by codifying egress fencing, placement SLOs, and tenant throttles in modular IaC.
- Scope includes Terraform modules, OPA/Conftest policies, Buildkite/GHA CI snippets, and runbook procedures. Does NOT cover: model-serving runtime internals or tenant billing reconciliation.

Ownership and stakeholders:
- Primary owner: eng-infra (allocator team) — Connor Mitchell (author)
- Secondary owners: cloud-accounts (networking), gpu-fleet (capacity), eng-sre (oncall/runbooks)
- Reviewers: Asha Patel (terraform platform), Diego Alvarez (networking), Megan Liu (sre)

High-level design and guarantees:
- The Burst Orchestrator is implemented as a small family of Terraform modules: allocator-core, allocator-pool, egress-shim, and ci-gate. Each module has explicit inputs for tenant-tagging, ci-safety-level, and capacity-profile.
- Safety guarantees provided by the catalog:
  - No module change may expand egress CIDR bindings without passing a restricted review (policy: egress-cidr-change).
  - New pool types must include a capacity-safety-config: {min_warm, max_spot, eviction_backoff_seconds}.
  - All deployments must pass a terraform-plan diff check and an OPA policy evaluation in CI.

Module catalog (names and primary inputs):
| Module name       | Purpose                                 | Key inputs (string names)                         | Outputs (brief)                 |
| allocator-core    | Shared resource definitions, tags, IAM  | org_id, environment, tenant_tag, kms_key_id      | vpc_id, allocator_service_account |
| allocator-pool    | Pool primitive for GPU pools            | pool_type, instance_profile, min_warm, max_spot  | pool_id, autoscaler_policy        |
| egress-shim       | Egress fencing and NAT / proxy binding | allowed_cidrs, nat_gateway, egress_label         | egress_attachment_id              |
| ci-gate           | CI integration and plan enforcement     | repo, branch_allowlist, opa_policy_bundle        | deployment_token                  |

Recommended pool_type values and semantics:
- reserved: backed by reserved capacity, low preemption, cost higher; suitable for enterprise Dedicated workloads.
- warm: pre-warmed fractional GPU sessions; cold start <200ms for KV cache seeding.
- spot: lowest-cost burst pool; best-effort preemptible VMs, eviction_backoff_seconds must be configured.

Example Terraform usage (simplified):
```hcl
module "allocator_core" {
  source      = "git::ssh://git@repo/redwood-iac//allocator-core?ref=v2025-01"
  org_id      = var.org_id
  environment = var.environment
  tenant_tag  = var.tenant
  kms_key_id  = var.kms_key
}

module "batch_warm_pool" {
  source         = "../allocator-pool"
  pool_type      = "warm"
  instance_profile = "g5-fractional"
  min_warm       = 8
  max_spot       = 0
  eviction_backoff_seconds = 600
}
```

Policy-as-code (OPA) highlights:
- OPA bundles live as part of the ci-gate module. Key policies: egress-cidr-change, pool-size-cap, iam-principal-least-privilege.
- Example policy check (pseudo):
  - deny[msg] { input.change.type == "egress"; not valid_egress(input.change) }

CI/CD pipeline contract and checks:
Every PR that touches allocator modules must include:
1) terraform fmt and terraform validate
2) terraform init + terraform plan (targeting a dry-run workspace)
3) OPA/Conftest evaluation of the plan JSON (policy exit code 0 required)
4) Unit tests for module helpers (terragrunt/terratest where applicable)
5) If the change alters egress allowed CIDRs or iam bindings, add a reviewer from cloud-accounts and security.

Minimal Buildkite snippet (example):
```yaml
steps:
  - label: "allocator: plan"
    command: |
      terraform fmt -check
      terraform init -backend-config="bucket=${TF_STATE_BUCKET}"
      terraform plan -out=plan.tfplan -input=false
      terraform show -json plan.tfplan > plan.json
      opa test -b policies/ plan.json || (echo "OPA failed"; exit 1)
```

Preflight validations (automated):
- Plan size limits: the plan must not create > 50 GPU instances in a single PR unless the change is flagged with emergency=true.
- Egress CIDR delta: any addition of public/0.0.0.0/0 or expansion beyond existing CIDR blocks triggers a mandatory review and security sign-off.
- Autoscaler sanity: min_warm <= max_capacity and max_spot < 4x(min_warm) by default; policy can override with documented rationale.

Canary rollout and rollback pattern (recommended):
1) Apply to a staging allocator in the same region: terraform apply -target=module.staging_pool
2) Observe warm-pool utilization, eviction rate, and egress session counts for 30m. Key metrics: evictions/min < 1, average token latency < 250ms, egress sessions stable.
3) Promote to 10% of tenant traffic via smart-routing flag for 2 hours. If errors or SLO breach, immediately run rollback step.
4) Full rollout only after 48 hours of stable metrics and sign-off from eng-sre.

Rollback runbook (emergency):
1) Hit the CI/CD manual rollback job: builds/promote-rollback with the previous release tag.
2) If the previous tag is unavailable, run terraform apply using the prior state snapshot: terraform apply -state=backup-<timestamp>.tfstate
3) Drain affected pool: kubectl annotate nodes retriable=false && run drain script to migrate sessions.
4) Open incident and route to oncall with runbook link.

Operational playbook and run commands:
- Quick health checks (run daily pre-shift):
  - curl -s https://telemetry.internal/allocator/summary | jq .pools
  - check: pool_warm_fill_ratio > 0.6 and evictions_5m < 3
- Emergency scaling (manual):
  - terraform apply -target=module.allocator-pool["emergency-burst"] -var emergency=true
  - post-apply: trigger autoscaler reconcile: curl -XPOST https://allocator.internal/reconcile
- Reassign egress: run egress attach: `./bin/egress-attach --pool-id $POOL_ID --cidr $CIDR --dry-run` then remove dry-run after verification.

Metrics, Alerts, and SLOs (examples):
- SLO: 95th-token-latency < 600ms for warm pools (monthly, per-tenant)
- Alert: evictions_rate_5m > 5 for any pool -> P1 oncall within 15m
- Alert: terraform_plan_failures > 3 per hour in ci-gate -> infra_eng triage, investigate flakiness

Testing matrix (scenarios and acceptance criteria):
- Scenario: New warm pool variant (g6-fractional)
  - Tests: unit module tests, plan pass, canary staging apply, evictions < 1/hour, latency within baseline
- Scenario: Egress CIDR expansion request
  - Tests: policy denies automatic merge, requires manual approval, pen-test review if adding public ranges
- Scenario: Large capacity increase (> 50 GPUs)
  - Tests: requires load-forecast doc, cost-owner approval, automatic debt ticket creation

Operational costs and labels to set for billing/tagging (required tags):
- tag:tenant, tag:billing_center, tag:project, tag:environment, tag:pool_type
- Cost control: pool budgets must be declared in the pool module via pool_budget_monthly (string amount).

Appendix: troubleshooting checklist (quick):
- If canary shows high evictions: reduce spot allocation and increase min_warm, rerun reconcilers.
- If CI OPA fails on an unrelated policy: comment on PR with `//opa:ignore <policy>` and request policy owner review.
- For emergency network misconfiguration: detach egress-shim and attach temporary NAT with limited CIDRs, escalate to cloud-accounts.

If you are making changes to any allocator-related module, follow the CI contract above and add the appropriate reviewers. For questions or to request exceptions, open a request with eng-infra and include telemetry snapshots and terraform plan JSON.
